promise: A Zero Carbon Act setting a net-zero 2050 target, plus an independent Climate Change Commission
made: 2017 election; Labour–Green confidence and supply agreement (Oct 2017)
detail: This was the Greens' central 2017 demand, and it was written into the support agreement. James Shaw, as Minister for Climate Change, introduced the bill on 8 May 2019. It passed on 7 November 2019 with almost unanimous support. Shaw had to accept a compromise: biogenic methane got a separate, weaker target of 24–47% below 2017 levels by 2050, instead of net zero. The framework still stands. However, on 13 October 2025 the National-led government lowered the methane target to 14–24%.

promise: A referendum on legalising personal cannabis use by the 2020 election
made: 2017 election; Labour–Green confidence and supply agreement
detail: The referendum was held with the general election on 17 October 2020, so the commitment was met. The proposal was defeated: in the official count about 50.7% voted against and about 48.8% in favour. Recreational cannabis therefore stayed illegal. The Greens' 2026 platform still calls for decriminalising personal use.

promise: Legal access to medicinal cannabis
made: 2017 election (Green member's bill inherited by Chlöe Swarbrick from Julie Anne Genter)
detail: The Green member's bill was defeated at its first reading in January 2018. The government's own medicinal cannabis law passed in December 2018. Swarbrick then worked on the regulations that followed. The outcome was delivered, but in a narrower form than the Greens proposed.

promise: Make drug checking (pill testing) legal
detail: In late 2021 New Zealand became the first country to make drug checking permanently legal, after temporary legislation in 2020. The law was a Labour government measure, passed while the Greens were in the cooperation agreement. We could not retrieve a source in this pass that credits the change specifically to Swarbrick or to the Greens, so treat the attribution as unconfirmed.

promise: Light rail to Auckland Airport
made: 2017 election (Labour pledge; light rail and rail/cycling investment were in the Labour–Green agreement)
detail: No line was built in six years of Labour-led government (2017–23). In January 2022 the government endorsed a $14.6 billion tunnelled scheme, and Auckland Light Rail Ltd was set up. The incoming National-led government stopped the project in November 2023. A Cabinet paper said about $228m had been spent 'without a metre of track laid'. The main responsibility lay with Labour ministers, but the Greens had campaigned on the project and it was in their agreement.

promise: A 'Green Transport Card' to cut public transport costs for people on low incomes
detail: It came late and in a smaller form. Half-price public transport for everyone was a temporary cost-of-living measure in 2022–23. In February 2023 the government made discounted fares permanent for Community Services Card holders and tertiary students, from 1 July 2023. That was close to six years after the agreement.

promise: Overhaul the welfare system: remove 'excessive' sanctions and substantially lift incomes
made: 2017 election (Metiria Turei's welfare policy); Labour–Green agreement
detail: Main benefits rose by $25 a week from April 2020. From 2021 they were indexed to wages, and Budget 2021 added a further $32–55 a week, fully in place by 2022. RNZ reported this reversed the 1991 benefit cuts in real terms. The agreement also promised to remove 'excessive' sanctions; we did not verify in this pass how many were removed. The rises still fell well short of what the Greens campaigned for: a large benefit rise in 2017, and a $385-a-week Guaranteed Minimum Income in 2023. Green critics inside and outside the party said the Greens accepted too little.

promise: Warm, dry rental homes (healthy homes standards)
detail: The Healthy Homes Guarantee Act 2017 was a Labour bill that the Greens supported. It passed in the government's first months and requires rental homes to meet heating, insulation and ventilation standards.

promise: Stronger renters' rights, including limits on rent rises and an end to no-cause evictions
detail: Labour's 2020 tenancy law banned rental bidding and ended no-cause evictions. It limited rent increases to once every 12 months, but did not cap their size, which the Greens wanted. The National-led government restored 90-day no-cause terminations in December 2024. For 2026 the Greens are again promising a cap on annual rent rises (2%) and a rental warrant of fitness.

promise: Re-establish a Mental Health Commission
detail: Following the mental health inquiry, the government created Te Hiringa Mahara, the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission.

promise: Double the refugee quota
made: 2017 election ('Greens would double refugee quota as priority')
detail: In September 2018 the government announced the quota would rise to 1,500 a year from 2020. Labour had joined the 'Double the Quota' campaign. Resettlement was then paused at the COVID-19 border closure and restarted in 2021. The Greens' 2026 platform promises a further increase.

promise: End new offshore oil and gas exploration
detail: In April 2018 the government banned new offshore oil and gas exploration permits. Shaw called it the 'nuclear-free moment of our generation'. The decision was Labour's, in a government the Greens supported.

promise: Bring agriculture into emissions pricing (pricing of farm emissions by 2025)
made: 2017 Green climate policy (Kiwi Climate Fund); government pledge in 2019 while Shaw was Climate Change Minister
detail: The 2019 government pledge was to price farm emissions by 2025. No price was in place when Labour left office in 2023. In June 2024 the National-led government confirmed it would keep agriculture out of the ETS. The Greens never had the numbers to force this, but it was the main gap in Shaw's climate record. The 2017 'Kiwi Climate Fund' dividend was never adopted.

promise: Strengthen New Zealand's 2030 Paris target (Shaw as Climate Change Minister)
made: 2020–23 cooperation agreement (Shaw kept the climate portfolio)
detail: In October 2021, before the Glasgow COP26 summit, the government raised its 2030 target from a 30% to a 50% cut in net emissions relative to 2005 gross emissions. How much of the target will be met by buying offshore emission reductions rather than cutting emissions at home remained contested.

promise: Incentives to switch to clean vehicles (Clean Car Discount / feebate)
detail: The Clean Car Discount ran from July 2021 to 31 December 2023. Low-emission vehicles got rebates, funded by fees on high emitters. EVs rose from about 6% of new car sales when it started to about 27% by the end of 2023. The National-led government repealed it under urgency on 14 December 2023, against the votes of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. The scheme was delivered, then reversed by the next government.

promise: Oppose 'waka-jumping' laws that let party leaders expel MPs from Parliament
made: Long-standing Green position (opposed the 1999, 2001 and 2005 bills)
detail: Bound by its 2017 agreement to let the Labour–NZ First coalition deal be implemented, the Green caucus voted for the Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Bill at every stage in 2018. It passed 63–57. A party spokesperson said the negotiators 'forgot' to register the Greens' opposition. Former co-leader Jeanette Fitzsimons publicly opposed the bill. In 2020 the Greens voted for a National bill to repeal the law (NZ First's Winston Peters called them 'untrustworthy'), and they voted for repeal again in 2021. In October 2024 the Greens used the same law to expel Darleen Tana from Parliament.

promise: No state funding for private schools (Green education policy)
detail: In August 2020 Shaw, as Associate Finance Minister, secured $11.7m from the COVID 'shovel-ready' fund for the private Green School in Taranaki. Newshub reported he had refused to sign off the $3b package unless the school was included. Former Green MPs called it a betrayal. Shaw apologised for an 'error of judgment', and in November 2020 the grant was converted into a loan.

promise: A wealth tax
detail: Not delivered. During the campaign Jacinda Ardern ruled out a wealth tax while she was Prime Minister. Labour then won an outright majority, and the 2020 cooperation agreement did not include one. The Greens had no leverage. They have campaigned for a wealth tax at every election since.

promise: 2023 tax plan: 2.5% wealth tax on net assets over $2m ($4m for couples), 45% top rate over $180,000, and a $385-a-week Guaranteed Minimum Income
detail: Not delivered: the Greens went into opposition. The 2026 tax plan, released early by mistake on 21 June 2026, is much less ambitious, and the NZ Herald said the party had 'dramatically reined in' its plans. The wealth tax now applies only to assets over $10m. The new top bracket starts at $160,000, and a $10,000 tax-free threshold remains. A broad commitment to raise benefits continues.

promise: Will not seek to govern with National
made: 2017 election aftermath (Shaw); repeated in every campaign since
detail: Shaw ruled out talks with National in 2017, and the Greens have only ever supported Labour-led governments. In February 2026 Hipkins, Swarbrick and Davidson announced at Waitangi that Labour and the Greens would work together in the campaign and in a future government. (The Greens did sign a policy memorandum of understanding with National in 2009, without giving it confidence and supply.)

promise: Restore New Zealand citizenship to Samoans born 1924–1949 (Teanau Tuiono's member's bill)
detail: Tuiono's Restoring Citizenship bill passed into law on 20 November 2024 with unanimous support from all parties. It is the Greens' most significant legislative win from opposition.

promise: A 'right to repair' law (Marama Davidson's member's bill)
detail: It passed its first reading on 19 February 2025 with Green, Labour, Te Pāti Māori and NZ First votes. NZ First later withdrew its support at select committee, so the bill no longer had a majority. Davidson also apologised in October 2025 for missing the bill's member's-day speaking slot. It has not passed.

promise: Revoke coal, gold and seabed-mining consents granted under the Fast-track Approvals Act, and repeal the Act
detail: A pledge for a future government. The Greens told mining companies they were 'on notice'.

promise: 2026 tax plan: 2.5% tax on net wealth over $10m, an inheritance tax, a 33% company rate for big corporations, a new bracket over $160,000 and a $10,000 tax-free threshold
detail: Pitched as tackling 'inequality and corporate greed' and paying for income-tax cuts for lower earners. National ran a social-media attack video claiming the Greens would tax income over $160,000 at 45%. Swarbrick said the video misrepresented the policy and called it 'AI slop'; National declined to remove it.

promise: Cap annual rent increases (2%), create a rental warrant of fitness and build tens of thousands of public homes
detail: The Greens have pushed for rent caps since at least 2020. Labour did not adopt them in 2017–23.

promise: 'KiwiMart': a government-owned supermarket chain made up of 120 stores and two distribution centres that Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell
detail: Pitched as a way to break the supermarket duopoly.

promise: 'Kiwipower', a new Crown entity investing in renewable generation to cut power bills, and 'electrify everything'
detail: Developed after the 2026 fuel shock linked to the Iran war.

promise: Restore the previous free school lunches scheme and expand it to about 400 more schools
detail: This would reverse the coalition's cheaper redesign of Ka Ora, Ka Ako.

promise: Restore pay equity and fund a settlement of at least $4.5b for 65,000 care and support workers
detail: Responds to the coalition's 2025 changes to the pay-equity regime.

promise: $4b for intercity passenger rail (an overnight Auckland–Wellington service, Christchurch–Dunedin trains, Te Huia extended to Tauranga)
detail: Comes alongside promises of fare-free public transport for young people, disabled people and Community Services Card holders, and a $2 adult fare cap.

promise: Cap political donations at $30,000, ban corporate donations, create a lobbying register and require a two-year stand-down before ministers can become lobbyists
detail: Builds on Golriz Ghahraman's Electoral (Strengthening Democracy) bill, which was defeated in 2022.

promise: Automatic (default) union membership for new workers
detail: Taken to the election as a member's bill.
